'''Game theory''' is the field of [[applied mathematics]] that [[Mathematical model|models]] interactions between multiple [[Agent-based model|agents]] as "games" of [[Strategy (game theory)|strategy]] between "players". It is a scientific method of describing, predicting, evaluating, and selecting choices (or "actions"), often with the view of maximising [[utility]] outcomes (or "payoffs") for one or more players.<ref name="Myerson">{{cite book|last=Myerson|first=Roger B.|author-link=Roger B. Myerson|year=1991|title=Game Theory: Analysis of Conflict|publisher=Harvard University Press|isbn=9780674341166}}</ref>

Game theory has applications in the [[Natural science|natural]], [[Formal science|formal]] and [[Social science|social sciences]],<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Shapley |first1=Lloyd S. |last2=Shubik |first2=Martin |date=1971-01-01 |title=Game Theory in Economics |chapter = Chapter 1, Introduction, The Use of Models |url=https://www.rand.org/pubs/reports/R0904z1.html |access-date=23 April 2023 |archive-date=23 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230423130243/https://www.rand.org/pubs/reports/R0904z1.html |url-status=live }}</ref> including [[biology]], [[computer science]], [[economics]], [[law]], [[logic]], [[political science]], [[systems science]], and [[philosophy]]. Subfields of game theory include [[algorithmic game theory]], [[behavioral game theory]], [[combinatorial game theory]], [[evolutionary game theory]], and [[quantum game theory]].

In 1994, the [[Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences|Nobel Prize in economics]] was awarded to the mathematician [[John Forbes Nash Jr.|John Nash]], the philosopher [[John Harsanyi]], and the economist [[Reinhard Selten]] for their pioneering work in game theory.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 1994 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/1994/press-release/ |access-date=2026-09-11 |website=NobelPrize.org |language=en-US}}</ref> Since then, game theorists who were awarded the Nobel include [[Thomas Schelling]] and [[Robert Aumann]] (2005),<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |title=Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2005 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2005/popular-information/ |access-date=2026-09-11 |website=NobelPrize.org |language=en-US}}</ref> [[Leonid Hurwicz]], [[Eric Maskin]], and [[Roger Myerson]] (2007),<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |title=Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2007 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2007/popular-information/ |access-date=2026-09-11 |website=NobelPrize.org |language=en-US}}</ref> [[Alvin E. Roth]] and [[Lloyd Shapley|Lloyd S. Shapley]] (2012),<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |title=Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2012 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2012/popular-information/ |access-date=2026-09-11 |website=NobelPrize.org |language=en-US}}</ref> [[Jean Tirole]] (2014),<ref name=":10">{{Cite web |title=Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2014 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2014/summary/ |access-date=2026-09-11 |website=NobelPrize.org |language=en-US}}</ref> and [[Paul Milgrom]] and [[Robert B. Wilson]] (2020).<ref name=":11">{{Cite web |title=Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2020 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2020/press-release/ |access-date=2026-09-11 |website=NobelPrize.org |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Overview and terminology ==
In game theory, a "game" is an abstract, mathematical representation of an interaction between agents ("players"), meant to capture the most basic properties of the game, namely: 

* the "players"; 
* the choices or actions available to each player;
* the value (or "payoff") that each player will receive for every possible strategy (i.e. a combination of actions of a given player in response to a given situation);<ref name="EGTLibreTexts" />
* the information each player has at the time of making their decisions; 

[[Eric Rasmusen]] refers to these four "essential elements" by the acronym "PAPI".<ref name="r7a2">{{cite book |last=Rasmusen |first=Eric |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5XEMuJwnBmUC&pg=PR5 |title=Games and Information |date=2007 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=978-1-4051-3666-2 |edition=4th}}</ref><ref name="r7b2">{{cite book |last1=Kreps |first1=David M. |author-link=David M. Kreps |title=Game Theory and Economic Modelling |date=1990 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-828381-2 |doi=10.1093/0198283814.001.0001}}{{page needed|date=July 2024}}</ref><ref name="r7c2">{{cite book |title=Handbook of Game Theory with Economic Applications |date=1992 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-0-444-89427-4 |editor1-last=Aumann |editor1-first=R. J. |editor2-last=Hart |editor2-first=S.}}{{page needed|date=July 2024}}</ref><ref name="r7d2">{{cite book |last1=Aumann |first1=Robert J. |title=Handbook of Game Theory with Economic Applications Volume 3 |last2=Heifetz |first2=Aviad |year=2002 |isbn=978-0-444-89428-1 |volume=3 |pages=1665–1686 |chapter=Chapter 43 Incomplete information |doi=10.1016/S1574-0005(02)03006-0}}</ref>

=== History ===
The significance of the work of the early game theorists in economics was its formalisation of strategic interaction, equilibrium concepts, and rational choice behavior, under the assumptions of perfect rationality, self-interest, complete information, and fixed game structure.<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last=Roszkowska |first=Ewa |date=2025-11-29 |title=Generalized Game Theory in Perspective: Foundations, Developments and Applications for Socio-Economic Decision Models |journal=Information |language=en |volume=16 |issue=12 |pages=1041 |doi=10.3390/info16121041  |doi-access=free|issn=2078-2489 }}</ref> Game theory as a field had its genesis in the 1944 book ''[[Theory of Games and Economic Behavior]]'', written by mathematicians [[John von Neumann]] and [[Oskar Morgenstern]]. The book built upon von Neumann's earlier work, which used the [[Brouwer fixed-point theorem]] on continuous mappings into compact [[Convex set|convex sets]], a method that later became standard in game theory and [[mathematical economics]].<ref name="NeumannMorgenstern">{{Cite book |last1=Neumann |first1=John von |url=https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691130613/theory-of-games-and-economic-behavior |title=Theory of Games and Economic Behavior |last2=Morgenstern |first2=Oskar |date=2007-04-08 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-0-691-13061-3 |access-date=23 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230328004503/https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691130613/theory-of-games-and-economic-behavior |archive-date=28 March 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref> In 1994, the Nobel Prize in economics was awarded to the game theorists [[John Forbes Nash]], [[Reinhard Selten]], and [[John Harsanyi]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name="EGTLibreTexts">{{cite web |date=2023-03-13 |title=1.1: Introduction to evolutionary game theory |url=https://math.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Applied_Mathematics/Agent-Based_Evolutionary_Game_Dynamics_%28Izquierdo_Izquierdo_and_Sandholm%29/01%3A_Introduction/1.01%3A_Introduction_to_evolutionary_game_theory |access-date=2026-09-10 |website=Mathematics LibreTexts |df=ymd-all}}</ref>

Initially, as a field of [[applied mathematics]], game theory was used in economics to describe and predict the behaviors of firms, markets, and consumers. The use of game theory in the social sciences has since expanded, with game theory later being widely applied in the analysis of political, sociological, psychological, and animal behaviours.<ref name="Larson2">{{cite journal |last1=Larson |first1=Jennifer M. |date=11 May 2021 |title=Networks of Conflict and Cooperation |journal=Annual Review of Political Science |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=89–107 |doi=10.1146/annurev-polisci-041719-102523 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Friedman1998">{{Cite journal |last=Friedman |first=Daniel |date=1998 |title=On economic applications of evolutionary game theory |url=https://leeps.ucsc.edu/media/papers/EconAppEvolGameTheory3-1-98.pdf |url-status=live |journal=Journal of Evolutionary Economics |volume=8 |pages=14–53 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140211210314/http://leeps.ucsc.edu/media/papers/EconAppEvolGameTheory3-1-98.pdf |archive-date=2014-02-11}}</ref> Modern academic research finds applications of game theory in fields as broad as [[international relations]], [[network science]], [[Voting system|voting systems]], [[linguistics]], [[law]], [[distributed control]], [[policy design]], [[Competition law|competition regulations]], [[project management]], and [[military technology]].<ref name="EGTLibreTexts" /><ref name="Piraveenan2019">{{cite journal |last1=Piraveenan |first1=Mahendra |date=2019 |title=Applications of Game Theory in Project Management: A Structured Review and Analysis |journal=Mathematics |volume=7 |issue=9 |page=858 |doi=10.3390/math7090858 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Game theory has also been used to develop theories of ethical or normative behavior and to [[Decision theory#Normative and descriptive decision theory|prescribe]] such behavior.<ref name="Camerer20032">{{cite book |last=Camerer |first=Colin F. |author-link=Colin F. Camerer |url=http://press.princeton.edu/chapters/i7517.html |title=Behavioral Game Theory: Experiments in Strategic Interaction |date=2003 |pages=5–7 |chapter=1.1 What Is Game Theory Good For? |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110514201411/http://press.princeton.edu/chapters/i7517.html |archive-date=14 May 2011}}</ref><ref name="KadaneLarkey1983">{{cite journal |last1=Kadane |first1=Joseph B. |last2=Larkey |first2=Patrick D. |date=December 1983 |title=The Confusion of Is and Ought in Game Theoretic Contexts |journal=Management Science |volume=29 |issue=12 |pages=1365–1379 |doi=10.1287/mnsc.29.12.1365}}</ref> In [[economics and philosophy]], scholars have applied game theory to help in the understanding of good or proper behavior. Game-theoretic approaches have also been suggested in the [[philosophy of language]] and [[philosophy of science]].<ref name="DeBruin2005">{{cite journal |last1=Bruin |first1=Boudewijn de |date=September 2005 |title=Game Theory in Philosophy |journal=Topoi |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=197–208 |doi=10.1007/s11245-005-5055-3}}</ref>

=== Theory and methodology ===
The main branches of economic theory are game theory, [[decision theory]], [[Mechanism design|mechanism design theory]], and [[general equilibrium theory]]. Unlike game theory, which analyses multi-agent interactions, decision theory focuses on [[Preference (economics)|preferences]] and the formation of beliefs within single-player scenarios. Decision theory is often used in the form of [[decision analysis]], which shows how best to acquire information before making a decision. Mechanism design theory is closely related to game theory, although the former is more focused on about the consequences of different types of rules, whereas the latter often takes the rules of the game as given. Areas of focus within mechanism design include [[Financial compensation|compensation]], [[Wage|wages]], [[risk]], [[Incentive|incentives]], and [[Auction|auctions]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=What is Game Theory? |url=http://www.dklevine.com/general/whatis.htm |access-date=2026-09-13 |website=www.dklevine.com}}</ref> Within game theory and mechanism design, a [[metagame]] refers to a game that aims to develop rules for the target or subject game, being applied in the contexts of [[metagame analysis]], and [[confrontation analysis]].{{sfnp|Howard|1971}}

Although game theory has broad application in general equilibrium theory, general equilibrium economists are usually concerned with [[Macroeconomics|macroeconomic]] issues of [[trade]] and [[Production (economics)|production]] in scenarios with a very large number of individual [[Consumer behaviour|consumers]] and [[Product (business)|producers]]. In particular, the theory of [[dynamic stochastic general equilibrium]] (DSGE) is applied, often in combination with game theoretic methods, to issues of [[investment management]], [[political economy]], [[Industrial organization|industrial organisation]], [[international trade]], and [[Monetary policy|monetary]], [[Fiscal policy|fiscal]], and [[tax policy]].<ref name=":4" /> 

As an [[economic methodology]], game theory provides a framework for the analysis of decision-making processes involving multiple stakeholders, each with conflicting or cooperative objectives. Unlike traditional [[Econometric model|econometric models]] that are descriptive (in the sense of predicting future outcomes based on historical data and statistical trends between variables) and [[Optimization problem|optimisation algorithms]] (which assume static environments and generally address single-objective problems within predefined constraints), game theory is inherently dynamic and accounts for the strategic interactions among participants. Game theory can further be applied in simulation-based approaches, such as [[Agent-based model|agent-based modeling]], in order to replicate market dynamics and policy outcomes under different scenarios by way of modelling reward-punishment mechanisms, competition for limited resources, and coalition formation.<ref name=":16">{{Cite journal |last1=Lefeng |first1=Cheng |last2=Mengya |first2=Zhang |last3=Pengrong |first3=Huang |last4=Wentian |first4=Lu |date=2025 |title=Game-Theoretic Approaches for Power-Generation Companies' Decision-Making in the Emerging Green Certificate Market |url=https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/17/1/71 |journal=Sustainability |language=en |volume=17 |issue=1 |issn=2071-1050}}</ref>

=== Games ===
A game is ''[[Cooperative game theory|cooperative]]'' if the players are able to form binding commitments externally enforced (e.g. through [[contract law]]). A game is ''[[Non-cooperative game|non-cooperative]]'' if players cannot form alliances or if all agreements need to be [[Self-enforcing agreement|self-enforcing]] (e.g. through [[Credible threat|credible threats]]).<ref>{{cite web |last=Shor |first=Mike |title=Non-Cooperative Game |url=http://www.gametheory.net/dictionary/Non-CooperativeGame.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140401211601/http://www.gametheory.net/Dictionary/Non-CooperativeGame.html |archive-date=1 April 2014 |access-date=2016-09-15 |website=GameTheory.net}}</ref>

A [[symmetric game]] is a game where each player earns the same payoff when making the same choice. The identity of the player does not change the resulting game facing the other player, and the game looks the same to all players.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Shor |first=Mike |date=2006 |title=Symmetric Game |url=https://www.gametheory.net/dictionary/Games/SymmetricGame.html |website=Game Theory.net}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=2021-08-17 |title=3.7: Undercut |url=https://math.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Applied_Mathematics/Introduction_to_Game_Theory%3A_A_Discovery_Approach_%28Nordstrom%29/03%3A_Repeated_Two-Person_Zero-sum_Games/3.07%3A_Undercut |access-date=2026-09-11 |website=Mathematics LibreTexts |df=ymd-all}}</ref> Formally, a symmetric two-player game can be defined as one where the matrix of one player's payoffs is the [[transpose]] of the other player's payoffs.<ref>{{cite web |date=2019-05-17 |title=2.5: The Transpose |url=https://math.libretexts.org/Courses/Mission_College/MAT_04C_Linear_Algebra_%28Kravets%29/02%3A_Matrices/2.05%3A_The_Transpose |access-date=2026-09-11 |website=Mathematics LibreTexts |df=ymd-all}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-01-24 |title=3.5: Properties of endorelations |url=https://math.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Combinatorics_and_Discrete_Mathematics/A_Cool_Brisk_Walk_Through_Discrete_Mathematics_(Davies)/03%3A_Relations/3.5%3A_Properties_of_endorelations |access-date=2026-09-11 |website=Mathematics LibreTexts |language=en}}</ref>{{Payoff matrix|Name=An asymmetric game|2L=E|2R=F|1U=E|UL=1, 2|UR=0, 0|1D=F|DL=0, 0|DR=1, 2}}{{Payoff matrix |Name=A zero-sum game |2L=A |2R=B |1U=A |UL=–1, 1 |UR=3, −3 |1D=B |DL=0, 0 |DR=–2, 2}}[[Zero-sum game|Zero-sum games]] (or constant-sum games) are games in which choices by players can neither increase nor decrease the available resources. More informally, in such a game, a player benefits only at the equal expense of others.<ref>{{cite book |last=Owen |first=Guillermo |author-link=Guillermo Owen |title=Game Theory: Third Edition |publisher=Emerald Group Publishing |year=1995 |isbn=978-0-12-531151-9 |location=Bingley |page=11}}</ref> 

[[Simultaneous game|Simultaneous games]] are games where both players move simultaneously, such that all players are unaware of the actions of other players. [[Sequential game|Sequential games]] are games where players do not make decisions simultaneously, and player's earlier actions affect the outcome and decisions of other players.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Chang |first1=Kuang-Hua |title=Design Theory and Methods Using CAD/CAE |date=2015 |isbn=978-0-12-398512-5 |pages=39–101 |chapter=Decisions in Engineering Design |doi=10.1016/b978-0-12-398512-5.00002-5}}</ref>

Games typically are assumed to be finite and discrete, with a finite number of players, moves, events, and outcomes. Nonetheless, [[Continuous game|continuous games]] allow players to choose a strategy from a continuous strategy set. For example, [[Cournot competition]] is typically modeled with players' strategies being any non-negative quantities, including fractional quantities.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}}

==== Information ====
A game of [[complete information]] is one where every player knows the rules, strategies and payoffs available to the other players but not necessarily the actions taken.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mirman |first=Leonard |title=Perfect Information |publisher=Palgrave Macmillan |year=1989 |isbn=978-1-349-20181-5 |location=London |pages=194–195}}</ref> A [[Bayesian game]], in contrast, is a strategic game with incomplete information.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Osborne |first=Martin J |title=An Introduction to Game Theory |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2020 |pages=271–277}}</ref> 

A game with [[perfect information]] is a game of complete information that also has all players, at every move in the game, know the previous history of the game and all moves previously made by all other players.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Mirman |first1=Leonard J. |title=Game Theory |date=1989 |isbn=978-0-333-49537-7 |pages=194–198 |chapter=Perfect Information |doi=10.1007/978-1-349-20181-5_22}}</ref> An imperfect information game is played when the players do not know all moves already made by the opponent, which is the case in a simultaneous move game.<ref name=":22">{{Cite book |last=Gibbons |first=Robert |title=Game Theory for Applied Economists |publisher=Princeton University Press |year=1992 |isbn=0-691-04308-6 |location=Princeton, New Jersey |pages=14–17}}</ref>

Games will change significantly if they are [[Repeated game|repeated]], that is, if the players will interact with each other again in the future with the information they obtained from previous games. In future games, players may act in response to the way in which other players had acted in the past; and in present games, these other players may choose their actions in such a way to prevent them from being punished in future games but instead to reward the players based on their [[reputation]].<ref name=":4" /> For example, a potential strategy in repeated games, known as [[tit for tat]], is to cooperate as long as one’s opponent cooperates, and then to defect for some number of rounds so as to "punish" the defector before cooperating again.<ref name=":18">{{Cite journal |last=Heydari Fard |first=Sahar |date=2022-09-13 |title=Strategic injustice, dynamic network formation, and social movements |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s11229-022-03576-3 |journal=Synthese |volume=200 |issue=5 |pages=392 |doi=10.1007/s11229-022-03576-3 |issn=1573-0964}}</ref>

Examples of perfect-information [[Game|recreational games]] include [[tic-tac-toe]], [[Draughts|checkers]], [[chess]], and [[Go (board game)|Go]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Ferguson |first=Thomas S. |author-link=Thomas S. Ferguson |title=Game Theory |url=https://www.math.ucla.edu/~tom/Game_Theory/mat.pdf#page=56 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040730140255/http://www.math.ucla.edu/~tom/Game_Theory/mat.pdf |archive-date=2004-07-30 |publisher=UCLA Department of Mathematics |pages=56–57}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Mycielski |first=Jan |author-link=Jan Mycielski |title=Handbook of Game Theory with Economic Applications |year=1992 |isbn=978-0-4448-8098-7 |volume=1 |pages=41–70 |chapter=Games with Perfect Information |doi=10.1016/S1574-0005(05)80006-2}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=2 March 2017 |title=Infinite Chess |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN-I6u-AxMg&t=0m25s |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211028/PN-I6u-AxMg |archive-date=2021-10-28 |publisher=PBS Infinite Series}}{{cbignore}} Perfect information defined at 0:25, with academic sources {{ArXiv|1302.4377}} and {{ArXiv|1510.08155}}.</ref> [[Poker]] and [[Contract bridge|bridge]] are examples of games of imperfect information.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Owen |first=Guillermo |title=Game Theory: Third Edition |publisher=Emerald Group Publishing |year=1995 |isbn=978-0-12-531151-9 |location=Bingley |page=4}}</ref>

==== Rationality ====
Players in game theory are generally assumed to be [[Rational agent|rational agents]] in a formal, mathematical sense. Rational agents act as if they have consistent preferences and unlimited computational capacity to achieve their well-defined objectives, and they behave in a manner in order to obtain the maximum possible payoff.<ref name="EGTLibreTexts" /> Players are also assumed to be self-interested, with the structure of the game itself being fixed and closed, such that each player’s objective is to maximize expected utility, given the strategies chosen by others. In this regard, utility functions are [[Exogeny|exogenous]], typically one-dimensional, and stable over time.<ref name=":12" /> Game theoretic models also generally assume [[Common knowledge (logic)|common knowledge]] of rationality, such that players are rational; they also know that others are rational; and that this knowledge is shared recursively.<ref name="VKnightRationality" />

==== Von Neumann–Morgenstern utility ====
Formally, utility, in the [[Von Neumann–Morgenstern utility theorem|von Neumann-Morgenstern]] framework, can be defined as follows. Let <math>X</math> be a non-empty set of alternatives, such that <math>X</math> is the set <math>\Delta(Z)</math> of simple lotteries (i.e. probability distributions with finite support) on some non-empty set <math>Z</math> of sure outcomes. Given two alternatives <math>x,y\in X</math>, a utility function on <math>X</math> is a function <math>u\to\mathbb{R}</math> associating to each alternative <math>x\in X</math> a utility level <math>u(x)\in\mathbb{R}</math>. A utility function <math>u</math> on <math>X</math> is said to be a von Neumann Morgenstern (vNM) utility function if:<ref name=":20">{{Citation |last=Danan |first=Eric |title=Aggregating sets of von Neumann-Morgenstern utilities |date=2010 |editor-last=UMR 8174 |editor-first=Centre d'Economie de la Sorbonne-CES |url=https://shs.hal.science/halshs-00523448 |access-date=2026-09-15 |publisher=Centre d'Économie de la Sorbonne (CES - UMR8174) |last2=Gajdos |first2=Thibault |last3=Tallon |first3=Jean-Marc}}{{Creative Commons text attribution notice|cc=by4|from this source=yes}}</ref> 

<math>u(x)=\sum_{z\in Z}x(z)u(z) \qquad \forall x\in X</math>. 

Alternatively, consider <math>\lambda\in[0,1]</math>, such that the <math>\lambda</math>-mixture of <math>x</math> and <math>y</math>, denoted <math>x\lambda y</math>, can be defined such that<math>x\lambda y=\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y</math>. (Note that <math>x\lambda y\in X</math>.) Thus, the vNM utility function can be defined in the following way:<ref name=":20" />

<math>u(x\lambda y)=\lambda u(x)+(1-\lambda)u(y) \qquad \forall ~~ x,y \in X,~ \lambda \in [0,1]</math>

=== Strategies ===
A [[Strategy (game theory)#Pure and mixed strategies|pure strategy]] is a deterministic strategy, whereas a [[Strategy (game theory)#Pure and mixed strategies|mixed strategy]] is probabilistic. Games can be divided into strictly and non-strictly determined games, such that a non-strictly determined game possesses only mixed strategies, whereas a strictly determined game possesses pure strategies as well.<ref name="VKnightGames">{{cite web |title=Games - Game Theory |url=https://vknight.org/gtb/chapters/games/ |access-date=2026-09-10 |website=vknight.org |df=ymd-all}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=2020-03-22 |title=11.2: Non-Strictly Determined Games |url=https://math.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Applied_Mathematics/Applied_Finite_Mathematics_%28Sekhon_and_Bloom%29/11%3A_Game_Theory/11.02%3A_Non-Strictly_Determined_Games |access-date=2026-09-10 |website=Mathematics LibreTexts |df=ymd-all}}</ref> Only a strictly determined game possesses a [[saddle point]], that is, an equilibrium that represents the best strategies for all players.<ref>{{cite web |date=2020-03-22 |title=11.1: Strictly Determined Games |url=https://math.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Applied_Mathematics/Applied_Finite_Mathematics_%28Sekhon_and_Bloom%29/11%3A_Game_Theory/11.01%3A_Strictly_Determined_Games |access-date=2026-09-10 |website=Mathematics LibreTexts |df=ymd-all}}</ref>  

For a two-player game, a dominant strategy for a given player is a strategy that produces a better payoff than the other player; conversely, a dominated strategy is one that is always worse than the other player and therefore never rational to play.<ref>{{cite web |date=2020-03-22 |title=11.3: Reduction by Dominance |url=https://math.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Applied_Mathematics/Applied_Finite_Mathematics_%28Sekhon_and_Bloom%29/11%3A_Game_Theory/11.03%3A_Reduction_by_Dominance |access-date=2026-09-10 |website=Mathematics LibreTexts |df=ymd-all}}</ref><ref name="VKnightRationality">{{cite web |title=Rationality - Game Theory |url=https://vknight.org/gtb/chapters/rationalisation/ |access-date=2026-09-11 |website=vknight.org |df=ymd-all}}</ref>

==== Domination ====
Dominated strategies can be grouped into strictly and weakly dominated strategies. A strategy is strictly dominated if, no matter what the other players do, a player always receives a strictly higher payoff by playing another strategy. A weakly dominated strategy, on the other hand, is one that does at least as well as all other strategies, no matter what the other players do, and is strictly better than at least one other strategy.<ref name="VKnightRationality" />

Formally, for the two-player game <math>(A,B)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}_2</math>, a strategy <math>s</math> is strictly dominated by strategy <math>\bar{s}</math> if, for all strategies of the other player <math>t</math>, <math>u(s,t)<u(\bar{s},t)</math>,, where <math>u</math> represents the utility function. A strategy may be weakly dominated if, instead, <math>u(s,t)\leq u(\bar{s},t)</math> and there exists some value of <math>t'</math> such that <math>u(s,t')<u(\bar{s},t')</math>.<ref name="VKnightRationality" />

==== Equilibria ====
For any given game, a [[strategy profile]] (or strategy combination) is a combination of strategies, such that each player gets one strategy.<ref name="EGTLibreTexts" /> For example, in a 3-player game where the action set <math>\mathcal{A} </math> is such that <math>\forall i, \mathcal{A}_i = \{A,B\} </math>, a valid strategy profile might be <math>s = ((1,0),(1,0),(0,1)) </math>, indicating that players 1 and 2 choose A, and player 3 chooses B.<ref name="VKnightRationality" /> 

An equilibrium is a stable state in which either one outcome occurs or a set of outcomes occur with known probability.{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}} A [[Nash equilibrium]] is a particular type of equilibrium strategy profile where every player is [[Best response|best responding]] to the strategies of the others. In such a setting, no player has an incentive to unilaterally deviate from their choice. [[John Forbes Nash]] proved that at least one such equilibrium exists in any finite non-cooperative game.<ref name="Chandrasekaran">{{cite web |last=Chandrasekaran |first=Ramaswamy |title=Cooperative Game Theory |url=http://www.utdallas.edu/~chandra/documents/6311/coopgames.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160418101712/http://www.utdallas.edu/~chandra/documents/6311/coopgames.pdf |archive-date=2016-04-18 |publisher=University of Texas at Dallas}}</ref><ref name="Brandenburger">{{cite web |last=Brandenburger |first=Adam |title=Cooperative Game Theory: Characteristic Functions, Allocations, Marginal Contribution |url=http://www.uib.cat/depart/deeweb/pdi/hdeelbm0/arxius_decisions_and_games/cooperative_game_theory-brandenburger.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170829084624/http://www.uib.cat/depart/deeweb/pdi/hdeelbm0/arxius_decisions_and_games/cooperative_game_theory-brandenburger.pdf |archive-date=29 August 2017 |access-date=14 April 2020}}</ref>
== Representation of games ==
{{Payoff matrix|Float=right|Width=330|Name=Normal form or payoff matrix of a 2-player, 2-strategy game|2L={{color|#900|Player 2<br />chooses ''Left''}}|2R={{color|#900|Player 2<br />chooses ''Right''}}|1U={{color|#009|Player 1<br />chooses ''Up''}}|1D={{color|#009|Player 1<br />chooses&nbsp;''Down''}}|UL={{color|#009|'''4'''}}, {{color|#900|'''3'''}}|UR={{color|#009|'''–1'''}}, {{color|#900|'''–1'''}}|DL={{color|#009|'''0'''}}, {{color|#900|'''0'''}}|DR={{color|#009|'''3'''}}, {{color|#900|'''4'''}}}}Non-cooperative games can be broadly represented in two forms. Generally, [[Normal-form game|normal form]] is used to represent non-cooperative simultaneous games, and [[Extensive-form game|extensive form]] is used to represent non-cooperative sequential ones. Alternative representations also exist, for example, [[Cooperative game theory|characteristic function form]] is used to represent cooperative games. 

Every extensive-form game has an equivalent normal-form game, however, the transformation to normal form may result in an exponential blowup in the size of the representation, making it computationally impractical.{{sfnp|Shoham|Leyton-Brown|2008|p=35}}

=== Normal form ===
The normal form (or strategic form) game is usually represented by a [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] which shows the players, strategies, and payoffs. In [[linear algebra]] notation, a two-player normal-form game can be mapped by a matrix. A general matrix mapping rows (actions of the first player) and columns (actions of the second player) to pairs of payoff values can be represented as follows:<ref name="VKnightGames" />

<math display="block">
\Gamma =
\begin{bmatrix}
(u_1(r_1,c_1),u_2(r_1,c_1)) & (u_1(r_1,c_2),u_2(r_1,c_2)) & \cdots & (u_1(r_1,c_n),u_2(r_1,c_n)) \\
(u_1(r_2,c_1),u_2(r_2,c_1)) & (u_1(r_2,c_2),u_2(r_2,c_2)) & \cdots & (u_1(r_2,c_n),u_2(r_2,c_n)) \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
(u_1(r_m,c_1),u_2(r_m,c_1)) & (u_1(r_m,c_2),u_2(r_m,c_2)) & \cdots & (u_1(r_m,c_n),u_2(r_m,c_n))
\end{bmatrix}
</math>

where the set of actions (or action set) <math>A</math> available to each player are, respectively, <math>A_1 = \{r_i \mid 1 \leq i \leq m\}</math> and <math>A_2 = \{c_j \mid 1 \leq j \leq n\}</math>.

An alternative approach is to use two separate matrices: <math>M_r</math> for the row player and <math>M_c</math> for the column player, defined as follows:<ref name="VKnightGames" />

<math display="block">(M_r)_{ij} = u_1(r_i,c_j)
\qquad
(M_c)_{ij} = u_2(r_i,c_j)</math>

==== Prisoner's dilemma ====
{{main|Prisoner's dilemma}}
The most popular example of a normal-form game is [[Prisoner's dilemma]]. In the dilemma, there are two players who are both [[Aiding and abetting|accomplices]] to a crime. Both have been arrested and imprisoned, and they cannot communicate with each other, nor do they know what the other prisoner is doing. The police do not have sufficient evidence for a conviction, but the prisoners do not know this. Instead, they tell each prisoner that, if they confess to their crimes, they will get a lighter sentence. Each player may thus either inform on themselves and the other player, or they may remain silent. If neither confess, neither will go to jail; if both confess, they will get an ordinary sentence; however, if one confesses and the other does not, the confessor will get a short sentence while the denier will get a long one.{{sfn|Poundstone|1993|pp=8, 117}}

Despite the best possible outcome being the situation in which both parties refuse to confess, the [[dominant strategy]] for each individual player, no matter what a suspect believes his partner is going to do, is in fact to betray the other, which aligns with the [[sure-thing principle]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Rapoport |first1=Anatol |title=The New Palgrave Dictionary of Economics |date=1987 |isbn=978-1-349-95121-5 |pages=1–5 |chapter=Prisoner's Dilemma |doi=10.1057/978-1-349-95121-5_1850-1}}</ref> The utility of this illustration is that it demonstrates the conflict between the pursuit of individual, selfish goals and the common good of both parties, representing an issue present in a variety of [[Tragedy of the commons|public goods problems]].<ref name=":4" />{{Payoff matrix|Name=The prisoner's dilemma|2L=Cooperate|2R=Defect|1U=Cooperate|UL=-1, −1|UR=-10, 0|1D=Defect|DL=0, −10|DR=-5, −5}}

==== Formal definition ====
Formally, an <math>N</math>-player normal form game comprises:<ref name="VKnightGames" />

* A finite set of <math>N</math> players.
* An action set for the players: <math>\{A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_N\}</math>.
* A set of payoff functions for the player that maps action sets to <math>\mathbb{R}</math>: <math>u_i : A_1 \times A_2 \times \cdots \times A_N \to \mathbb{R}</math>.

A strategy <math>
\sigma

</math> for a player with action set <math>A</math> is a probability distribution over the elements of <math>A</math>, such that:<ref name="VKnightGames" />

<math>\sigma \in [0,1]_{\mathbb{R}}^{|A|}</math>, with <math>\sum_{i=1}^{|A|}\sigma_i=1</math>.

Given an action set <math>\mathcal{A}</math>, the set of valid strategies (also known as the strategic profile or strategic set) is denoted as <math>\Delta\mathcal{A}</math> so that:<ref name="VKnightGames" />

<math display="block">
\Delta\mathcal{A}
=
\left\{
\sigma \in [0,1]_{\mathbb{R}}^{|\mathcal{A}|}
\left|
\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal{A}|}\sigma_i = 1
\right.
\right\}

</math>

In order to calculate expected utility for a given action set,<ref name="VKnightGames" />

<math display="block">
u_i(\sigma_1,\sigma_2)
=
\sum_{a_1 \in \mathcal{A}_1}
\sum_{a_2 \in \mathcal{A}_2}
\sigma_1(a_1)\sigma_2(a_2)u_i(a_1,a_2)
</math>In [[Mathematical optimization|mathematical optimisation]], assuming complete information, a normal-form game can also be defined as follows:<ref name=":14">{{Cite journal |last=Pavel |first=Lacra |date=2026 |title=On Operator Theory and Applications in Game Theory |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-control-022624-033840 |journal=Annual Review of Control, Robotics, and Autonomous Systems |publisher=Annual Reviews |volume=9 |pages=99–122 |doi=10.1146/annurev-control-022624-033840 |issn=2573-5144}}</ref>

* Let I be a set of agents, <math>\mathcal{I}:=\{1,2,\ldots,N\}</math>.
* Each agent <math>i \in \mathcal{I}</math> chooses its decision variable (i.e., its strategy or action) <math>x_i</math> from its local decision set.
* Let Ω be a decision set, such that the local decision set <math>\Omega_i \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n_i}</math>, and <math>\Omega=\Omega_1\times\cdots\times\Omega_N\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n</math> is the overall decision space, and <math>n=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}n_i</math>.
* Let <math>x:=\begin{pmatrix}
x_1\\
\vdots\\
x_N
\end{pmatrix}
=\operatorname{col}((x_i)_{i\in\mathcal{I}})
\in\Omega</math> denote the stacked [[Vector space|vector]] of all agent decisions.

Thus, the game, <math>\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{I},(J_i)_{i\in\mathcal{I}},\mathcal{X})</math>, is then defined such that the goal of each agent <math>i\in\mathcal{I}</math> is to minimize its [[Loss function|objective function]] <math>J_i(x_i,x_{-i})</math>, which depends on both the local variable <math>x_i</math> and the decision variables of the other agents, <math>x_{-i}:=\operatorname{col}((x_j)_{j\in\mathcal{I}\setminus\{i\}})</math>.<ref name=":14" />

=== Extensive form ===
[[File:Ultimatum_Game_Extensive_Form.svg|right|thumb|An extensive form game, with players represented by numbers at the nodes and choices represented by letters at the lines]]
Extensive form games can be visualized using game [[Tree (graph theory)|trees]]. Within a tree, each [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|vertex]] (or node) represents a point of choice for a player; the lines out of the vertex represent a possible action for that player; [[Information set (game theory)|information sets]] are represented by dashed lines; and the payoffs are specified at the bottom of the tree, that is, being represented as the terminal nodes. The extensive form can be viewed as a multi-player generalization of a [[decision tree]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Fudenberg |first1=Drew |title=Game Theory |last2=Tirole |first2=Jean |date=1991 |publisher=MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-06141-4 |page=67}}</ref><ref name=":15">{{Cite web |last=Levine |first=David |author-link=David K. Levine |title=Dynamic Game Theory Readings |url=http://www.dklevine.com/econ211/readings.htm |access-date=2026-09-13 |website=www.dklevine.com}}</ref> 

Solving an extensive form game (that is, finding its Nash equilibrium) involves the use of [[Backward induction|backwards induction]], which involves the analysis of the tree from the end nodes to the root, removing or "pruning" dominated strategies at each information set.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Williams |first=Paul D. |title=Security Studies: an Introduction |publisher=Routledge |year=2013 |edition=second |location=Abingdon |pages=55–56}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Subgame Perfection - Game Theory |url=https://vknight.org/gtb/chapters/subgame-perfection/ |access-date=2026-09-11 |website=vknight.org |language=en}}</ref>

==== Battle of the sexes ====
{{main|Battle of the sexes (game theory)}}
{{Payoff matrix|Name=Battle of sexes (note that they both want to do the same action but have different preferences)|2L=Preferred Action (action1)|2R=Unpreferred action (action2)|DL=0,0|DR=2,1|1U=Unpreferred action (action1)|UL=1,2|1D=Preferred action (action2)|UR=0,0}}The "battle of the sexes" game involves two players of different sexes, arbitrarily chosen, each with a different set of preferences.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Battle of the Sexes {{!}} History, Participants, & Facts {{!}} Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/Battle-of-the-Sexes-tennis |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230423131644/https://www.britannica.com/topic/Battle-of-the-Sexes-tennis |archive-date=23 April 2023 |access-date=2023-04-23 |website=Encyclopædia Britannica}}</ref> [[File:PD_with_outside_option.svg|right|thumb|A game of imperfect information. The dotted line represents ignorance on the part of player 2, formally called an [[Information set (game theory)|information set]].]]

==== Formal definition ====
Formally, an <math>N</math>-player extensive form game with complete information is characterised by:<ref name="VKnightGames" />
* A finite set of players <math>\mathcal{N}</math> with <math>|\mathcal{N}| = N</math>.
* A tree <math>G = (V, E, x^0)</math> where:
** <math>V</math> is the set of vertices,
** <math>E</math> is the set of edges, and
** <math>x^0 \in V</math> is the root of the tree.
* A partition <math>(V_i)_{i \in \mathcal{N}}</math> of the non-terminal vertices, assigning each decision node to a player.
* A set <math>O</math> of possible outcomes.
* A function <math>u</math> mapping each terminal node (leaf) of <math>G</math> to an element of <math>O</math>.

A strategy for a player is a mapping from each information set to a probability distribution over the available actions at that set. Given a game in extensive form <math>(\mathcal{N}, G, (V_i)_{i \in \mathcal{N}}, O, u)</math>, the set of [[Information set (game theory)|information sets]] <math>\mathcal{V}_i</math> for player <math>i \in \mathcal{N}</math> is defined as a partition of <math>V_i</math>, such that each element of <math>\mathcal{V}_i</math> denotes a set of nodes at which the player cannot distinguish their exact location when choosing an action. Thus, every information set contains vertices for a single player, who has the move at that information set, and all vertices in an information set must have the same number of successors (with the same action labels).<ref name="VKnightGames" /><ref name=":15" />

Games of [[Information asymmetry|incomplete information]] can be reduced, within extensive form representations, to games of imperfect information by introducing "[[Move by nature|moves by nature]]",{{sfnp|Shoham|Leyton-Brown|2008|p=60}} that is, by characterising nature as a "player 0". Information sets belonging to nature <math>\mathcal{V}_0</math> are known as "singletons", with moves of nature regarded as behavior strategies, that is, strategies that map from information sets to probability distributions over feasible actions.<ref name=":15" />

=== Characteristic function form ===
{{main|Cooperative game theory}}
In cooperative game theory the characteristic function lists the payoff of each coalition. The origin of this formulation is in John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern's book.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-02-12 |title=Game theory – Von Neumann, Morgenstern, Theory {{!}} Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/science/game-theory/The-von-Neumann-Morgenstern-theory |access-date=2025-03-19 |website=Encyclopædia Britannica |language=en}}</ref>

Formally, a characteristic function is a function <math> v : 2^N \to \mathbb{R} </math><ref><math>2^N</math> denotes the [[power set]] of <math>N</math>.</ref> from the set of all possible coalitions of players to a set of payments, and also satisfies <math> v( \emptyset ) = 0 </math>. The function describes how much collective payoff a set of players can gain by forming a coalition.

=== Alternative game representations ===
{{see also|Succinct game}}
